Consistency.justification: The proposal aligns perfectly with the provided core idea, title, and keywords. It comprehensively integrates all the required components: recurrence matrices, change-in-quantile features, InceptionTime, ReliefF feature selection, and the specific semi-supervised learning paradigms (label propagation, label spreading, and self-training). The application to single-ended protection for PV-connected transmission lines using PSCAD/EMTDC simulations on WSCC 9-bus and IEEE 39-bus systems is also accurately reflected.

Clarity.justification: The research proposal is extremely clear and well-structured. The methodology transitions logically from data generation and feature construction to model selection and the semi-supervised pipeline. The algorithmic details, such as how recurrence plots are used to generate quantile-change features, are explicitly defined. The evaluation metrics and risk factors are also clearly articulated, leaving very little ambiguity about how the research will be conducted.

Novelty.justification: While the individual machine learning techniques (InceptionTime, recurrence plots, ReliefF, label propagation) are well-established, their specific combination is quite original in the context of power system protection. Using change-in-quantile features derived from recurrence plots as inputs to a deep time-series classifier, combined with a semi-supervised framework to address label scarcity for inverter-based resource protection, represents a strong application-driven innovation, even if it does not introduce a fundamentally new ML algorithm.

Soundness.justification: The proposal is highly rigorous. The data generation relies on industry-standard PSCAD/EMTDC simulations encompassing diverse fault scenarios and noise, which ensures realistic data. The experimental design is robust, featuring comprehensive baselines (both deep learning on raw waveforms and classical methods), thorough evaluation metrics (accuracy, precise fault location MAE, label efficiency curves), detailed ablation studies, and strict statistical rigor (multiple random seeds, significance testing).

Feasibility.justification: The project is highly feasible, relying on established simulation tools and open-source machine learning frameworks. The proposed pipeline uses relatively lightweight models (InceptionTime, ReliefF). The authors have astutely identified the primary feasibility risk: the computational latency of generating recurrence plots for real-time relay protection (which requires millisecond-level inference). Their proposed mitigations (small sliding windows, distance thresholding, and small quantile sets) demonstrate practical foresight, though real-time deployment will still require careful optimization.

Significance.justification: The proposal addresses a critical issue in modern power systems: the failure of traditional distance relays when dealing with the non-sinusoidal, low-magnitude fault currents generated by inverter-based resources like PV plants. Furthermore, addressing the realistic constraint of label scarcity in power grid disturbances through semi-supervised learning greatly increases the practical value and potential real-world impact of the proposed method.

strengths: Comprehensive and highly rigorous experimental design with realistic grid simulations.
Strong focus on a critical real-world constraint (label scarcity) via a well-defined semi-supervised pipeline.
Excellent integration of domain-specific feature engineering (recurrence-quantiles) with state-of-the-art deep time-series classification.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is mostly combinatorial and application-focused rather than introducing foundational ML advancements.
Meeting the strict real-time latency requirements for grid protection using recurrence plots and deep learning pipelines may pose engineering challenges during practical deployment.
